title: Q4 roadmap planning
scratchpad:
calendar: Larkspan not Orchardly (read-only API)
dash = 4 charts, one eng
cold start <4s, <3 = stretch
versioning doc: Jun
segments: Okay, I think that's everyone. Sam's dialing in from the car for the first bit, so if you hear a truck, that's him, not me.
Yeah, sorry, I'm on the way back from a customer visit. I'll stay muted when I'm not talking. Go ahead, Maya, I read the pre-read last night.
Great. So the goal for today is a first real cut of the Q4 roadmap. Themes first, then the actual bets, then what we're explicitly not doing.
In the doc I proposed three themes. Connect, which is integrations. See, which is reporting. And speed, which is basically the technician app.
Can I push on the names a little? Connect, see and speed sounds like something printed on a poster in a dentist's waiting room.
Ha, fair enough. The names really don't matter. I just want three or four buckets so we stop arguing about forty separate tickets one at a time.
Then I'd add a fourth bucket, honestly. Platform hygiene. API versioning, cleaning up the old endpoints, the stuff nobody ever puts on a slide.
Is that a theme, or is that just tax? I'm not against it, I just don't want it quietly eating the whole quarter while nobody's looking.
It's tax we've been skipping for two years. If we don't version the API before more partners show up, every single change gets harder.
And there's the legacy job export endpoint. My plan is to switch it off on the thirty-first of December, end of year, nice and clean.
Okay, if it's a real theme, I want it written down properly. Jun, can you get me a versioning proposal by next Friday, the second?
Probably, yeah. Teodor said he'd help me with the examples. Let's say the second of October for a first draft.
Good. Platform stays as a fourth theme for now, and we decide how much capacity it gets once everything else is on the table.
Do we actually know the capacity number yet? Last quarter we planned without one and ended up cutting things in week six, which was painful.
Roughly forty engineer weeks, after holidays and support duty. Maybe a bit more if nobody gets the flu in December, which never happens.
Okay, forty engineer weeks it is. Let's start with connect, because that's the one with an outside party and a clock on it. Marcus?
Sure. So two calendar vendors have reached out about a partner integration, Orchardly and Larkspan. I've had two calls with each of them now.
Orchardly is the bigger one by a mile. Lots of small service businesses use it, plumbers, cleaners, a ton of our prospects already live in it.
Larkspan is a lot smaller, but it's built for dispatch teams. Shared crew calendars, standby blocks, swapping shifts, that kind of thing.
And what do they actually want from us? Is this a logo in their marketplace, or a real two-way sync that we have to maintain forever?
Both want two-way sync. A job booked in Quillmark shows up on the technician's calendar, and time blocked on the calendar shows up as unavailable for dispatch.
My instinct going in was Orchardly. The reach is just so much bigger, and the sales team keeps hearing that name on discovery calls.
Same here. If we're only doing one, do the one with the most logos. We can always add the smaller one next year if it's worth it.
Before we lock that in, Hana spiked both APIs a couple of weeks ago. Hana, do you have your notes handy? I only skimmed them.
Somewhere, yes. Give me a few minutes to find the doc, I wrote it up in the sync channel and it's buried under a hundred other threads.
No rush. For now the tentative lean is Orchardly, and we come back to it when Hana finds the notes. Let's do the dashboard in the meantime.
Okay, reporting. This is the one customers ask about the most. I counted eleven accounts asking for some kind of dispatcher dashboard since July.
And what they want is pretty consistent. Jobs completed per day, first time fix rate, average travel time between jobs, and technician utilization.
Utilization is the scary one. Nobody agrees on how to calculate it, and every customer will tell us our number is wrong on day one.
We could show the inputs instead of one magic number. Hours booked, hours on site, hours driving. Let them do whatever math they believe in.
I like that a lot. Fewer opinions baked into the product. How many charts are we talking about for a first version, Marcus?
My draft spec has six. The four I just mentioned, plus jobs by status and a late arrivals chart, which dispatchers specifically asked for.
Six charts with filters by technician, crew and date range is not small, though. That's real query work, not just a pretty front end.
Some of those queries would hit the jobs table pretty hard. We'd want a reporting replica, otherwise dispatch slows down every Monday morning.
How long for a first version, roughly, if we do all six? I need a date I can say out loud to customers without crossing my fingers.
All six plus the replica, I'd say a beta around the twentieth of November. That's with two people on it the whole time, though.
Okay, let's write down the twentieth of November as a working date and revisit it after speed, because speed competes for the same people.
Speaking of which. Hana, you've been living inside the technician app lately. What does the performance picture actually look like?
Honestly, not great on older phones. Cold start on our reference Android phone, the cheap one from three years ago, is six point eight seconds.
On a recent iPhone it's under two seconds, so most of us never feel it. But a lot of crews are on hand-me-down Android phones.
That matches what I hear on calls. A technician opens the app in a driveway, it hangs, and they just phone the dispatcher instead.
Which kind of defeats the whole point of having the app, doesn't it. So what's the target we'd actually commit to?
I'd love to say under three seconds on the reference phone. That's the number I'd be proud of, and it's what the good apps do.
Under three is ambitious. About half of that start time is the map library initializing, and we don't own that code at all.
We could lazy load the map, though. Most technicians open the job list first anyway, the map comes later when they're driving.
Let's pencil in under three seconds for now, and Hana, think about whether the map trick really gets us there. We'll come back to it.
Will do. There's also the job list itself. It takes two point one seconds to render forty jobs, which is just silly, that's our own code.
Can I go back to the dashboard for a second? I talked to one of our bigger customers yesterday and they said something useful.
They said they'd happily take four charts in December over six charts in January. They just want something they can show their ops manager.
That's a really good signal, honestly. If we cut it down, which four would you keep? And don't say utilization is optional.
Jobs completed, first time fix, travel time, and the utilization inputs Hana suggested. Late arrivals and jobs by status can wait for a second version.
Four charts is a different project. If we also skip date range comparisons, I can probably do it without the reporting replica at first.
So what does that do to the date? Are we still talking about the twentieth of November, or does it move earlier?
Same date, the twentieth, but with one engineer instead of two. That frees someone up for the speed work, which I think matters more right now.
That's a good trade. Dashboard is four charts, beta on the twentieth of November, one engineer. Marcus, can you update the spec to match?
Yep, I'll cut the spec down to four charts today and send it around before the end of the day, with the other two marked as later.
Found my notes, by the way. Sorry, the search in that channel is terrible. Do you want the calendar stuff now while I have it open?
Yes, please, now's perfect. We left it at a tentative lean toward Orchardly, pending whatever you found in the spike.
So. Orchardly's API is read-only for partners right now. We can read events off the calendar, but we can't write jobs onto it.
They told me write access is on their roadmap, but when I asked for a date the answer was sometime next year, probably, maybe.
Read-only is half an integration. The whole pitch to customers is the job showing up on the technician's calendar automatically.
Larkspan has full write access, webhooks for every change, and a sandbox I had working in about an hour. Their docs are honestly better than ours.
Ouch, okay. But what about reach? Larkspan has a fraction of Orchardly's users. Is it really worth a big chunk of our quarter?
The users they do have are exactly our buyers, though. Dispatch teams with crews. Orchardly's reach is mostly solo operators who'd never pay for us.
That's the part that changes my mind. A read-only integration aimed at the wrong audience is not the one we should build first.
So let's reverse what I said earlier. We go with Larkspan for the calendar integration, not Orchardly, and revisit Orchardly once they ship write access.
I'm fine with that. Can someone let the Orchardly folks down gently, though? I don't want to burn that bridge, they could matter next year.
I'll handle Orchardly. I'll tell them we're starting with someone else and want to talk again as soon as their write access ships.
And I'd put Teodor on the Larkspan build. He wrote our webhook layer, and Hana's notes give him a real head start.
Okay. Let's do the platform bucket properly, since Jun's been patient. Remind me what the actual versioning proposal is.
Right now we have one version of the API and we change it in place. Every breaking change turns into a negotiation with whoever's integrated.
I want dated versions, sent in a header. A partner pins a date, and we can change things without breaking anyone pinned to an older one.
As opposed to a version number in the path? That's exactly what the Larkspan people asked me about on the last call, actually.
Path versions are easier to explain, but they force a big bang migration every time. Dated headers let us move one endpoint at a time.
But on the proposal itself, the second of October isn't going to happen now that Teodor's on Larkspan. He was going to write half of it.
Okay, that's fair, things moved around today. What's a realistic date? I'd rather have a real date than a hopeful one.
I'll write the API versioning proposal myself and have it to you by Friday the ninth of October. That one I can actually hit.
The ninth works. Send it to the whole group, not just me. Marcus will want to read it before he talks to any more partners.
The other half of hygiene is that export endpoint I mentioned at the start. I pulled the logs while you were all talking about charts.
Fourteen customers still call it every week, and three of them hit it every single night from some script nobody on their side remembers writing.
Ugh. If we switch that off on the thirty-first of December, we find out whose scripts those are on New Year's Day, from very angry people.
And their IT person is probably on holiday until the second week of January. That's a terrible way to start the year with a customer.
Could we just give them a full quarter? Announce it in October, switch it off at the end of March. That's plenty of time for anyone.
I think that's right. Let's move the sunset to the thirty-first of March instead of December. The replacement export is already live, so there's no rush.
Fine by me. I mostly wanted a date that actually holds, and the thirty-first of March holds. I'll update the endpoint headers.
I'll write the deprecation email to those fourteen customers and get it out by the fifteenth of October, with the March date in it.
Thanks. Include the replacement endpoint and a link to the migration guide, so nobody has to email support just to figure it out.
Okay, back to the speed target. Hana, did you get a chance to think about the map trick while we were going?
A bit. Lazy loading the map saves maybe two seconds. The rest is our own startup work, and a big chunk of that is the sync on launch.
Realistically, with lazy loading and deferring the first sync, we'd land around three and a half seconds on the reference phone. Not three.
And getting from three and a half down to under three means rewriting the sync layer, which is not a Q4 project, whatever anyone says.
So under three seconds is a stretch goal at best. I don't want to commit to a number in front of customers that we already know we'll miss.
Agreed. Let's make the target under four seconds on the reference Android phone instead of three. Under three stays a stretch goal, not a commitment.
Under four I'm confident about. And I'll get the job list rendering under one second, that one's just bad code we wrote in a hurry.
Can I start telling customers about the speed work, or is that premature until we've actually shipped something they can feel?
Wait until we ship the first improvement. Under promise, over deliver. Okay, priorities, because we've got more than forty engineer weeks of stuff here.
Going in, my order was calendar, dashboard, speed, then platform. After today I think speed moves to the top, since it's what technicians feel every day.
I agree. Speed first, then the Larkspan integration, then the dashboard, and the platform work fits in around the edges of all three.
Platform isn't edges, but fine, as long as the versioning proposal and the deprecation actually happen. They both have dates now.
They will. One more thing, offline mode and SMS reminders both came up in the pre-read comments. Those need their own session, so I'm not touching them today.
Good. And nothing on this list depends on the Atlas launch going perfectly? I don't want the whole roadmap held hostage by launch week.
None of it does. The speed work and the Larkspan build can both start the week after next, regardless of what happens with the launch.
Great. I'll write up the roadmap doc with the four themes, the new order and the dates we agreed, and share it with everyone tomorrow.
Can you put the Orchardly reversal in there with the reasoning? Sales is definitely going to ask why we picked the smaller one.
Yes, I'll spell it out. Read-only API, wrong audience. Okay, thanks everyone, that was a good session. Sam, drive safe.

items.text: Partner with Larkspan for the calendar integration instead of Orchardly; revisit Orchardly once it ships write access
Technician app cold start target is under four seconds on the reference Android phone; under three seconds is a stretch goal
Legacy job export endpoint sunsets on March 31 instead of December 31
Dashboard first version is four charts, beta November 20 with one engineer
Q4 priority order: speed, then the Larkspan integration, then the dashboard, with platform work around them
Write the API versioning proposal by Friday, October 9
Email the fourteen customers still using the export endpoint by October 15, with the March date
Cold start on the reference Android phone is 6.8 seconds today

enhanced.markdown: **Calendar integration: Larkspan, not Orchardly.** Hana's spike found Orchardly's partner API is read-only, with write access only vaguely promised for next year, while Larkspan has full write access, webhooks for every change and a working sandbox. Larkspan's users are dispatch teams with crews, our buyers. Revisit Orchardly once it ships write access; Marcus lets Orchardly down gently, and Teodor builds the Larkspan integration.

**Speed and dashboard:** Cold start on the reference Android phone is 6.8 seconds today. The target is under 4 seconds; under 3 stays a stretch goal, not a commitment. Hana will also get the job list rendering under one second. Dashboard v1 is four charts (jobs completed, first time fix, travel time and the utilization inputs), with a beta on November 20 and one engineer.

**Platform and priorities:** The Q4 order is speed, then the Larkspan integration, then the dashboard, with platform work around them. Jun writes the API versioning proposal (dated versions sent in a header) by Friday, October 9. The legacy job export endpoint sunsets on March 31 instead of December 31; Marcus emails the fourteen customers still calling it by October 15, with the March date.
Roadmap doc: spell out why Larkspan over Orchardly for sales (read-only API, wrong audience).
